claims.text: Rapid quenching of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 produces a predominantly amorphous microstructure.
The rapidly quenched amorphous Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 microstructure is metastable and has limited thermal stability.
A controlled sub-Tg anneal immediately after quenching will improve amorphous retention in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
The sub-Tg anneal will delay crystallization onset during subsequent reheating.
Sub-Tg annealing reduces residual internal stresses in the quenched amorphous alloy.
Sub-Tg annealing decreases excess free volume in the quenched amorphous alloy.
Reducing residual stress and free volume lowers the density of crystallization nucleation sites in the amorphous matrix.
Below Tg, controlled atomic rearrangements can relieve stress and eliminate excess free volume without causing crystallization.
The relaxation produced by sub-Tg annealing diminishes the driving force for crystallization during thermal cycling.
The annealed alloy will exhibit a simpler and more robust thermal response than untreated Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Crystallization of an amorphous alloy appears as an exothermic event in DSC, allowing its onset temperature to be measured.
The untreated Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy has a complicated thermal response involving multiple transformations and cooling-dependent behavior.
Crystallization in untreated Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 occurs at temperatures lower than its melting transitions.
Cooling rate changes the phase-transformation temperatures of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Cooling rates of approximately 10^5–10^6 K/s are appropriate for producing the initial amorphous Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 state.
Exceeding Tg or annealing for too long can induce crystallization rather than stabilization.
If the initial cooling rate does not produce a metastable amorphous state, post-quench sub-Tg annealing will not provide the expected benefit.
XRD can be used to evaluate relative amorphous and crystalline phase content after treatment.
TEM can assess the distribution and density of potential crystallization nucleation sites.
